summary: Children measure the SAME object in two different units and discover the inverse relationship: the smaller the unit, the more of them it takes, so the larger the number. A desk measures about 120 in centimetres but only about 47 in inches — the desk hasn't changed; the count is bigger because a centimetre is smaller than an inch. This bridges from 'counting units' to understanding that a measurement is a number relative to a unit. The ~120/~47 figures are illustrative of one real desk, not fixed for every object.
misconceptions: Bigger-unit-bigger-number: believes the larger unit (inch) gives the larger number because inches are 'bigger'.
Thinks the object itself is longer when the number is bigger — the cm measurement 'makes the desk longer'.
Smaller-unit-smaller-number: reasons a centimetre is small so it must give a small number, landing on inches.
Treats equal counts as equal lengths regardless of unit size (10 small clips = 10 jumbo clips).

activities.title: One desk, two rulers: watch the counts differ
steps: Before measuring, PREDICT: which number will be bigger when you measure the desk in centimetres versus inches? Say WHY.
Lay the inch ruler along the desk edge and count units as a tally climbs to about 47.
Lay the centimetre ruler along the very same edge and watch the tally race past to about 120.
Point to what actually changed between the two measurements — and confirm the desk itself did not change.
Toggle to a third, larger unit (metres) and watch the count shrink; say whether that fits the rule.
Complete the statement frame: 'smaller unit → ____ units → ____ number' and 'larger unit → ____ units → ____ number'.
activities.insight: A measurement is a number relative to a unit: the smaller the unit, the more of them fit, so the larger the number — even though the object is unchanged.

activities.title: Same count, different length: the paperclip chains
steps: Compare object A, measured as 10 regular paperclips, with object B, measured as 10 jumbo paperclips.
Decide whether the two objects are the same length, and explain why or why not.
Lay the two chains alongside each other to check the prediction.
activities.insight: Equal counts do NOT mean equal lengths when the units differ in size — unit size is critical in measurement, unlike in counting discrete items.

activities.title: Check and consolidate the inverse relation
steps: Answer: which gives the bigger number for the same desk — centimetres or inches — and say why.
Answer: measure the desk in metres instead of centimetres — will the number be bigger or smaller? Why?
Answer the paperclip item: object A is 10 small clips, object B is 10 jumbo clips — same length or not, and why?
Review a side-by-side reference of the desk labelled '120 cm / 47 in' (illustrative of one real desk) and reveal the rule: 'smaller unit → more of them → bigger number'.
activities.insight: The learner can predict and justify measurement outcomes from unit size across new units, not just recall the desk result.

checkQuestion: Here is a desk. If you measure it in centimetres you get one number, and if you measure the SAME desk in inches you get a different number. Which measurement will be the BIGGER number — the centimetres or the inches? And why?
checkAnswer: The centimetres give the bigger number, because a centimetre is smaller than an inch, so it takes MORE centimetres than inches to cover the same desk (smaller unit → more units → bigger number).
